input_json: {"title":"Database Systems and Design","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This course provides a comprehensive introduction to database systems, covering both theoretical foundations and practical implementation skills essential for modern software development. Students will explore relational database design principles, SQL programming, database normalization, transaction management, and performance optimization techniques. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on experience with industry-standard database management systems including MySQL and PostgreSQL, while also introducing NoSQL databases like MongoDB for modern web applications. Through real-world projects, students will design and implement database solutions for business scenarios, learning to balance performance, security, and scalability requirements. The course integrates current industry practices including database security, backup strategies, and cloud database deployment. Students will work both individually and in teams to develop database-driven applications, preparing them for software engineering roles, data analyst positions, or advanced coursework in data science and distributed systems. By the end of the quarter, students will have built a portfolio demonstrating proficiency in database design, query optimization, and full-stack application development with database integration.","learning_objectives":["Students will design normalized relational database schemas to solve complex business data management problems using entity-relationship modeling and normalization principles","Students will implement advanced SQL queries and stored procedures through hands-on practice with MySQL and PostgreSQL database management systems","Students will analyze database performance bottlenecks by examining query execution plans, indexing strategies, and transaction isolation levels","Students will develop full-stack web applications using modern frameworks like Node.js or Django that integrate seamlessly with both relational and NoSQL databases"],"prerequisites":"Completion of CS 162 (Data Structures and Algorithms) with grade C+ or better, CS 161 (Introduction to Programming II), and MATH 231 (Discrete Mathematics). Students must demonstrate proficiency in at least one programming language (preferably Python, Java, or JavaScript) and have basic understanding of software development lifecycle and version control systems like Git.","target_audience":"Undergraduate computer science majors in their sophomore or junior year who have completed foundational programming courses and are pursuing careers in software engineering, web development, data analysis, or database administration. Ideal for students planning to work in technology companies, financial services, healthcare IT, or those considering graduate studies in data science or information systems."}

input_json: {"title":"Advanced Machine Learning Systems Design","domain":"computer_science","level":"graduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This graduate-level course focuses on the design, implementation, and deployment of large-scale machine learning systems in production environments. input_json: {"title":"Advanced Machine Learning Systems and Scalability","domain":"computer_science","level":"graduate","duration":"semester","description":"This graduate-level course explores the design, implementation, and deployment of machine learning systems at scale. Students will examine the complete ML pipeline from data ingestion to model serving, focusing on distributed computing frameworks, model optimization techniques, and production deployment strategies. The course covers advanced topics including federated learning, edge computing for ML, automated machine learning (AutoML), and MLOps practices. Students will work with industry-standard tools such as Apache Spark, TensorFlow Extended (TFX), Kubernetes, and cloud-based ML platforms. Through hands-on projects, students will design and implement scalable ML architectures that can handle real-world data volumes and traffic patterns. Topics include distributed training algorithms, model compression and quantization, A/B testing for ML systems, monitoring and observability, and ethical considerations in large-scale ML deployment. Prior coursework in machine learning fundamentals (equivalent to CS 4/229 Machine Learning) with hands-on experience in Python, TensorFlow or PyTorch. Ideal candidates are those seeking to transition from academic or small-scale ML projects to enterprise-level system design and implementation."}

input_json: {"title":"Advanced Machine Learning Systems Design","domain":"computer_science","level":"graduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This graduate-level course focuses on the engineering and architectural aspects of deploying machine learning systems at scale. Students will explore the complete lifecycle of ML systems, from data pipeline design and model training infrastructure to deployment, monitoring, and maintenance in production environments. The course bridges the gap between theoretical machine learning knowledge and practical implementation challenges faced in industry settings. Topics include distributed training frameworks, model serving architectures, MLOps practices, data versioning, experiment tracking, A/B testing for ML models, and system reliability considerations. Students will work with cloud platforms, containerization technologies, and modern ML infrastructure tools while developing a comprehensive understanding of performance optimization, scalability, and security in ML systems. This course is essential for students pursuing careers as ML engineers, data scientists in production environments, or research scientists working on large-scale systems. input_json: {"title":"Advanced Machine Learning for Big Data Analytics","domain":"computer_science","level":"graduate","duration":"semester","description":"This graduate-level course provides comprehensive coverage of advanced machine learning techniques specifically designed for large-scale data processing and analysis. Students will explore distributed computing frameworks, scalable algorithms, and cloud-based machine learning platforms to handle datasets that exceed traditional computational limitations. The curriculum emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical implementation, covering topics including distributed gradient descent, ensemble methods for big data, deep learning on distributed systems, and real-time streaming analytics. Students will gain hands-on experience with industry-standard tools such as Apache Spark, Hadoop ecosystem, TensorFlow Distributed, and cloud ML services from AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure. The course addresses critical challenges in modern data science including data preprocessing at scale, feature engineering for high-dimensional datasets, model deployment in production environments, and performance optimization. input_json: {"title":"Statistical Methods for Data Science","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course provides undergraduate students with a comprehensive foundation in statistical concepts and methods essential for data science applications. Students will explore descriptive and inferential statistics, probability distributions, hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and statistical modeling techniques commonly used in data-driven decision making. The course emphasizes practical application through hands-on analysis of real-world datasets from various domains including business, healthcare, and social sciences. Students will learn to interpret statistical results, assess data quality, and communicate findings effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences. Key topics include exploratory data analysis, correlation and causation, linear and multiple regression, ANOVA, chi-square tests, and bootstrap methods. The course integrates statistical theory with computational practice using statistical software packages. Students will develop critical thinking skills to evaluate statistical claims, design appropriate analyses for different data types, and understand the limitations and assumptions of statistical methods. This course serves as a crucial bridge between introductory statistics and advanced data science techniques, preparing students for careers in analytics, research, business intelligence, and graduate studies in data science or related fields.","learning_objectives":["Students will apply descriptive and inferential statistical methods to analyze real-world datasets and draw meaningful conclusions for business and research applications","Students will evaluate statistical assumptions and model validity through diagnostic plots, residual analysis, and goodness-of-fit tests using R and Python","Students will design appropriate statistical tests and analyses by identifying data types, research questions, and selecting suitable methodologies for different scenarios","Students will communicate statistical findings using visualization tools, written reports, and oral presentations tailored to diverse stakeholder audiences"],"prerequisites":"MATH 151 (Calculus I), STAT 201 (Introduction to Statistics), and CS 101 (Introduction to Programming) or equivalent. Students should have basic familiarity with algebraic concepts, fundamental programming logic, and introductory statistical concepts including measures of central tendency, variability, and basic probability.","target_audience":"Undergraduate students majoring in Data Science, Computer Science, Mathematics, Business Analytics, or related quantitative fields who seek to develop strong statistical foundations for data analysis careers or graduate studies. Ideal for students planning to work as data analysts, business analysts, research associates, or pursue advanced degrees in data science."}

input_json: {"title":"Advanced Machine Learning for Big Data Analytics","domain":"computer_science","level":"graduate","duration":"semester","description":"This graduate-level course provides comprehensive coverage of advanced machine learning techniques specifically designed for large-scale data analysis. Students will explore scalable algorithms, distributed computing frameworks, and cloud-based solutions essential for modern data science applications. The curriculum emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical implementation of machine learning models on big data platforms including Apache Spark, Hadoop ecosystem, and cloud services like AWS and Google Cloud Platform. Students will work with real-world datasets exceeding traditional computational limits, learning to optimize model performance, handle data preprocessing at scale, and deploy production-ready solutions. Key topics include ensemble methods, deep learning architectures for big data, stream processing, feature engineering at scale, and AutoML systems. The course bridges the gap between academic machine learning concepts and industry requirements, preparing students for senior data scientist and machine learning engineer roles. Through hands-on projects using industry-standard tools and frameworks, students will develop expertise in designing, implementing, and maintaining machine learning pipelines that can process terabytes of data efficiently. This course is essential for data science professionals seeking to advance their careers in organizations dealing with massive datasets and complex analytical challenges.","learning_objectives":["Students will design and implement scalable machine learning algorithms to process datasets exceeding 100GB using distributed computing frameworks","Students will optimize model performance and resource utilization through advanced hyperparameter tuning and distributed training techniques on cloud platforms","Students will evaluate and compare ensemble methods, deep learning architectures, and automated machine learning approaches by implementing comprehensive benchmarking studies","Students will deploy end-to-end machine learning pipelines using Apache Spark, MLflow, and containerization technologies like Docker and Kubernetes"],"prerequisites":"Completion of introductory machine learning course (CS/STAT 5XX level), proficiency in Python programming including pandas, scikit-learn, and NumPy libraries, solid understanding of linear algebra and statistics, experience with SQL databases, and familiarity with command-line interface and version control systems (Git). Prior exposure to cloud computing platforms recommended but not required.","target_audience":"Graduate students in Data Science, Computer Science, Statistics, or related quantitative fields with 1-2 years of machine learning experience. Ideal for students pursuing careers as senior data scientists, machine learning engineers, or data architects in technology companies, financial institutions, healthcare organizations, or research facilities that handle large-scale data operations."}

input_json: {"title":"Applied Statistical Analysis for Data Science","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This course provides undergraduate students with essential statistical foundations and practical analytical skills required for modern data science applications. Students will gain proficiency in industry-standard tools while building a portfolio of statistical analyses that demonstrate their ability to extract actionable insights from complex data. input_json: {"title":"Data Visualization and Statistical Graphics","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This course introduces students to the principles and practice of creating effective data visualizations for exploratory analysis, statistical communication, and data-driven storytelling. Students will learn to transform raw data into compelling visual narratives using industry-standard tools and programming libraries. The course covers visualization theory, including perception psychology and design principles, while providing hands-on experience with statistical graphics, interactive dashboards, and web-based visualizations. Students will work with real-world datasets from various domains including business, healthcare, and social sciences to create visualizations that reveal patterns, trends, and insights. Emphasis is placed on choosing appropriate chart types, designing for different audiences, and avoiding common visualization pitfalls. The course balances theoretical foundations with practical application, preparing students to communicate data findings effectively in professional settings. Projects include creating static visualizations, interactive dashboards, and presentation-ready graphics. Students will develop a portfolio of visualization work that demonstrates their ability to translate complex data into accessible visual stories. input_json: {"title":"Statistical Methods for Data Analysis","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This foundational course introduces students to essential statistical concepts and methodologies used in data science applications. Students will learn to apply statistical techniques to real-world datasets, develop critical thinking skills for data interpretation, and gain hands-on experience with statistical software. The course covers descriptive statistics, probability distributions, hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and statistical modeling. Emphasis is placed on understanding when and how to apply different statistical methods, interpreting results in context, and communicating findings effectively. Students will work with datasets from various domains including business, healthcare, social sciences, and technology to develop practical skills in statistical analysis. This course serves as a crucial foundation for advanced data science coursework and prepares students for entry-level analyst positions in industry. Students should have basic familiarity with spreadsheet software and fundamental mathematical concepts including functions, derivatives, and basic probability. Ideal for students in their sophomore or junior year who have completed basic mathematics requirements and are preparing for internships or advanced coursework in machine learning and predictive analytics."}

input_json: {"title":"Advanced Topics in Algebraic Topology","domain":"mathematics","level":"graduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This graduate-level course explores advanced concepts in algebraic topology, building upon fundamental knowledge of homology and cohomology theory. Students will delve into spectral sequences, characteristic classes, K-theory, and cobordism theory, with applications to differential geometry and mathematical physics. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and computational techniques, preparing students to engage with current research in topology and related fields. Topics include the Serre spectral sequence, Chern classes, vector bundles, and stable homotopy theory. Students will develop expertise in advanced topological invariants and their applications to classification problems in geometry and topology. The course includes a significant research component where students will read recent papers and present original investigations. This coursework is essential for students pursuing doctoral research in topology, algebraic geometry, or theoretical physics, and provides critical background for understanding modern developments in homotopy theory and its connections to number theory and representation theory.","learning_objectives":["Students will construct and compute spectral sequences to solve complex homological problems in algebraic topology and differential geometry","Students will analyze characteristic classes and vector bundle theory through detailed calculations using Chern-Weil theory and obstruction theory","Students will prove fundamental theorems in K-theory and cobordism by applying advanced techniques from stable homotopy theory","Students will demonstrate research proficiency using contemporary mathematical software including SageMath and specialized topology packages for computational verification of theoretical results"],"prerequisites":"Completion of graduate-level courses in algebraic topology (covering fundamental groups, homology, and cohomology), abstract algebra (including module theory over principal ideal domains), and real analysis. Students must have proven competency with category theory fundamentals and familiarity with basic differential geometry. Prior coursework in complex analysis and functional analysis strongly recommended. Students should demonstrate comfort with proof-writing at the graduate level.","target_audience":"Second or third-year mathematics PhD students specializing in topology, geometry, or related areas, as well as advanced master's students planning to pursue doctoral studies. Students should have strong backgrounds in abstract algebra and point-set topology, with career goals in academic research, government research laboratories, or advanced positions in mathematical modeling and data science requiring sophisticated topological methods."}

input_json: {"title":"Real Analysis I","domain":"mathematics","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This foundational course in real analysis introduces students to the rigorous theoretical underpinnings of calculus and mathematical analysis. Students will explore the structure of real numbers, sequences, series, limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration from a proof-based perspective. The course emphasizes developing mathematical maturity through constructing formal proofs and understanding abstract mathematical concepts. Topics include the completeness axiom, convergence of sequences and series, uniform convergence, properties of continuous functions on closed intervals, the mean value theorem, and the fundamental theorem of calculus with rigorous proofs. Students will learn to write clear, logically sound mathematical arguments and develop critical thinking skills essential for advanced mathematics. This course serves as a bridge between computational mathematics and abstract mathematical theory, preparing students for graduate study in mathematics, careers in mathematical research, actuarial science, or fields requiring strong analytical reasoning skills. The course builds essential skills in logical reasoning, proof techniques, and mathematical communication that are fundamental to success in pure and applied mathematics.","learning_objectives":["Students will construct rigorous epsilon-delta proofs to demonstrate understanding of limits, continuity, and differentiability in real analysis","Students will analyze convergence properties of sequences and series through formal proof techniques including comparison tests, ratio tests, and root tests","Students will evaluate the completeness of the real number system by proving fundamental theorems such as the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem and intermediate value theorem","Students will apply advanced proof methods using mathematical software like LaTeX to typeset formal mathematical arguments and communicate complex theoretical concepts"],"prerequisites":"Completion of Calculus I, II, and III (or Multivariable Calculus) with grades of C or better, and either Introduction to Mathematical Proofs or Discrete Mathematics. Students should be comfortable with basic proof techniques including direct proof, proof by contradiction, and mathematical induction. Familiarity with set notation, functions, and elementary number theory is expected.","target_audience":"Mathematics majors in their sophomore or junior year who have completed the calculus sequence and are preparing for advanced undergraduate or graduate-level mathematics courses. Also suitable for physics, engineering, or computer science students seeking rigorous mathematical foundations for theoretical work or graduate study."}

input_json: {"title":"Linear Algebra and Matrix Theory","domain":"mathematics","level":"undergraduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This course provides a comprehensive introduction to linear algebra and matrix theory, fundamental mathematical tools essential for advanced mathematics, engineering, computer science, economics, and data science. Students will explore vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and matrix decompositions through both theoretical analysis and computational applications. The course emphasizes developing mathematical reasoning skills while building practical competency in solving systems of linear equations, performing matrix operations, and understanding geometric interpretations of linear algebraic concepts. Students will work with real-world applications including computer graphics transformations, principal component analysis, least squares regression, and network analysis. The course integrates technology through computational software like MATLAB or Python to visualize concepts and solve complex problems. Students should be comfortable with algebraic manipulation, basic trigonometry, and have exposure to formal mathematical reasoning and notation.","target_audience":"Undergraduate students in mathematics, engineering, computer science, physics, or economics who have completed introductory calculus and are preparing for advanced coursework requiring linear algebra. Ideal for students planning careers in data science, engineering, research, or graduate study in STEM fields."}

input_json: {"title":"Linear Algebra with Applications","domain":"mathematics","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course provides a comprehensive introduction to linear algebra with emphasis on both theoretical foundations and practical applications across multiple disciplines. Students will explore vector spaces, linear transformations, matrix operations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and orthogonality. The course bridges abstract mathematical concepts with real-world applications in computer science, engineering, physics, economics, and data science. Through computational exercises using MATLAB or Python, students will solve systems of linear equations, perform matrix decompositions, and analyze linear models. Topics include Gaussian elimination, determinants, basis and dimension, diagonalization, and least squares approximation. Students will develop critical thinking skills through proof-writing exercises and gain practical experience through projects involving data analysis, computer graphics transformations, and optimization problems. This course serves as essential preparation for advanced mathematics courses including differential equations, numerical analysis, and abstract algebra, while also providing foundational knowledge for machine learning, quantum mechanics, and econometrics. By the end of the semester, students will possess both the theoretical understanding and computational skills necessary to apply linear algebra concepts in their chosen field of study.","learning_objectives":["Students will analyze systems of linear equations to solve real-world problems in engineering, economics, and computer science using matrix methods and Gaussian elimination","Students will compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors through hand calculations and computational software to understand dynamic systems and data dimensionality reduction","Students will construct mathematical proofs by applying fundamental theorems of linear algebra including the rank-nullity theorem and spectral theorem","Students will implement matrix operations and decompositions using MATLAB or Python to process datasets and perform numerical computations in scientific applications"],"prerequisites":"Completion of Calculus I and II (MATH 1251 and 1252) with grades of C or better, and either Discrete Mathematics (MATH 2300) or Introduction to Mathematical Reasoning (MATH 2200). Students should be comfortable with algebraic manipulation, basic proof techniques, and have familiarity with functions and graphing.","target_audience":"Second or third-year undergraduate students majoring in mathematics, computer science, engineering, physics, or economics who seek to develop advanced mathematical reasoning skills and computational proficiency. Ideal for students planning graduate study in STEM fields or careers in data science, software engineering, research, or quantitative analysis."}

input_json: {"title":"Advanced Topics in Algebraic Topology","domain":"mathematics","level":"graduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This graduate-level course explores advanced concepts in algebraic topology, focusing on spectral sequences, characteristic classes, and modern computational methods. Students will develop expertise in homological algebra techniques applied to topological problems, including the construction and application of Serre and Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequences. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical applications in geometric topology, differential geometry, and mathematical physics. Students will engage with current research literature and learn to apply sophisticated topological invariants to classify spaces and maps. Topics include fiber bundles, vector bundles, Chern classes, Stiefel-Whitney classes, and cobordism theory. The curriculum integrates traditional proof-based approaches with modern computational topology tools, preparing students for research in pure mathematics, theoretical physics, or data science applications. Through rigorous problem-solving and independent research projects, students will develop the mathematical maturity necessary for doctoral research or advanced positions in academia and industry. This course serves as essential preparation for students pursuing dissertations in topology, geometry, or related fields, while also providing valuable background for those applying topological methods in applied mathematics, computer science, or engineering disciplines.","learning_objectives":["Students will construct and analyze spectral sequences to compute homology and cohomology groups of complex topological spaces in algebraic topology research contexts","Students will evaluate characteristic classes of vector bundles through explicit calculations using Chern-Weil theory and cohomological methods","Students will prove fundamental theorems in fiber bundle theory by applying advanced techniques from homological algebra and differential geometry","Students will implement computational topology algorithms using Python and SageMath to verify theoretical results and explore conjectures in modern research problems"],"prerequisites":"Completion of undergraduate real analysis, abstract algebra, and point-set topology. Graduate-level algebraic topology covering fundamental groups, covering spaces, homology theory, and cohomology theory. Familiarity with category theory and basic homological algebra including exact sequences, chain complexes, and derived functors. Mathematical maturity equivalent to passing graduate qualifying examinations in analysis and algebra.","target_audience":"Graduate students in mathematics, mathematical physics, or related fields who have completed foundational courses in algebraic topology and seek advanced research preparation. input_json: {"title":"Database Systems and Design","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This course provides a comprehensive introduction to database systems, covering both theoretical foundations and practical implementation skills essential for modern software development. The curriculum emphasizes real-world applications through projects involving database design for web applications, data analysis, and business intelligence scenarios. By integrating theoretical concepts with practical programming assignments, students develop the critical thinking and technical skills necessary for roles in software engineering, data analysis, and system administration. input_json: {"title":"Statistical Learning and Predictive Modeling","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This course provides undergraduate students with a comprehensive introduction to statistical learning methods and their applications in data science. Students will explore both supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, including linear and logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, clustering algorithms, and dimensionality reduction methods. The course emphasizes the practical application of these methods using real-world datasets from various domains such as business, healthcare, and social sciences. Students will learn to evaluate model performance, handle overfitting, and interpret results in meaningful ways. Through hands-on programming assignments and projects, students will develop proficiency in R and Python for implementing statistical learning algorithms. The course bridges theoretical foundations with practical implementation, preparing students for advanced data science coursework and entry-level positions in analytics, business intelligence, and data-driven decision making. Students should be comfortable with basic probability concepts, linear algebra fundamentals, and have experience writing functions and manipulating data structures in at least one programming language.","target_audience":"Undergraduate students majoring in Data Science, Statistics, Computer Science, or related quantitative fields who have completed introductory statistics and programming courses. Ideal for juniors and seniors preparing for careers in data analysis, business analytics, or graduate studies in data science or machine learning."}

input_json: {"title":"Advanced Machine Learning for Big Data Systems","domain":"computer_science","level":"graduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This graduate-level course explores cutting-edge machine learning techniques specifically designed for large-scale data systems and distributed computing environments. input_json: {"title":"Applied Statistics and Probability for Data Science","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course provides undergraduate students with a comprehensive foundation in statistical methods and probability theory essential for data science applications. By integrating statistical theory with computational tools like R and Python, students will develop the analytical skills necessary for roles in data analysis, business intelligence, and quantitative research. Students should have basic familiarity with algebraic concepts, functions, and at least one programming language (preferably Python or R). input_json: {"title":"Applied Data Analysis and Visualization","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This intermediate undergraduate course introduces students to the fundamental principles and practical applications of data analysis and visualization in modern data science. The course emphasizes hands-on experience with Python programming, data manipulation libraries, and visualization frameworks to solve authentic business and research problems. Through project-based learning, students will develop critical thinking skills for interpreting data patterns, identifying trends, and communicating insights effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences. The curriculum covers exploratory data analysis, statistical inference, hypothesis testing, and advanced visualization techniques including interactive dashboards. Students will work with diverse datasets from fields such as healthcare, finance, marketing, and social media to understand how data-driven decision making impacts various industries. input_json: {"title":"Advanced Topics in Algebraic Topology","domain":"mathematics","level":"graduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This graduate-level course provides an in-depth exploration of advanced concepts in algebraic topology, building upon fundamental knowledge of homology and homotopy theory. Students will examine spectral sequences, characteristic classes, K-theory, and cobordism theory, with emphasis on their applications to geometric problems and connections to other areas of mathematics. The course covers both classical results and contemporary developments, including computational aspects and modern research directions. Through rigorous theoretical development and problem-solving, students will gain proficiency in sophisticated topological techniques essential for research in topology, geometry, and mathematical physics. input_json: {"title":"Linear Algebra and Matrix Theory","domain":"mathematics","level":"undergraduate","duration":"quarter","description":"This course provides a comprehensive introduction to linear algebra with emphasis on both theoretical foundations and practical applications. Students will explore vector spaces, linear transformations, matrix operations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and systems of linear equations. Topics include Gaussian elimination, determinants, orthogonality, diagonalization, and the spectral theorem. The course emphasizes visual and geometric interpretations of algebraic concepts, helping students understand how linear algebra underlies many areas of modern mathematics and science. Through problem-solving sessions and collaborative projects, students will apply linear algebra techniques to model and solve problems in optimization, computer graphics, machine learning, and differential equations. input_json: {"title":"Data Structures and Algorithms","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamental data structures and algorithmic problem-solving techniques essential for computer science. input_json: {"title":"Data Structures and Algorithms","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamental data structures and algorithmic problem-solving techniques essential for computer science. Students will explore abstract data types including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation of these structures. Students will analyze algorithm efficiency using Big O notation and learn to select appropriate data structures for specific problems. Key algorithms covered include sorting (quicksort, mergesort, heapsort), searching (binary search, graph traversal), and basic dynamic programming. Through hands-on programming assignments, students will implement data structures from scratch and solve computational problems of varying complexity. The course balances mathematical rigor with practical coding skills, preparing students for advanced computer science coursework and technical interviews. Laboratory sessions provide guided practice with implementation challenges, while projects encourage creative application of learned concepts. By course completion, students will possess strong foundational knowledge for software development, system design, and algorithmic thinking that serves as a cornerstone for all subsequent computer science studies.","learning_objectives":["Students will implement and analyze the performance of fundamental data structures including linked lists, trees, hash tables, and graphs using appropriate programming languages.","Students will design and implement efficient algorithms for searching, sorting, and graph traversal problems while analyzing their time and space complexity using Big O notation.","Students will evaluate and select optimal data structures and algorithms for solving real-world computational problems based on performance requirements and constraints."],"prerequisites":"Introduction to Programming (CS 101), Discrete Mathematics, and proficiency in at least one programming language (Java, C++, or Python)","target_audience":"Second-year computer science majors and related engineering students who have completed introductory programming courses"}

input_json: {"title":"Distributed Consensus Mechanisms and Byzantine Fault Tolerance","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course explores the theoretical foundations of achieving agreement in distributed systems where components may fail or behave maliciously. Students will examine classical consensus protocols, Byzantine agreement algorithms, and modern blockchain consensus mechanisms through rigorous mathematical analysis. The curriculum covers impossibility results like the FLP theorem, practical algorithms such as PBFT and Raft, and emerging consensus paradigms including proof-of-stake and hybrid approaches. Emphasis is placed on formal verification techniques, complexity analysis, and theoretical bounds on fault tolerance. Students will analyze trade-offs between safety, liveness, and performance in various network models, from synchronous to partially synchronous environments. The course bridges foundational distributed systems theory with contemporary applications in cryptocurrency, distributed databases, and fault-tolerant computing. Through formal proofs, algorithm analysis, and theoretical exercises, students develop deep understanding of why certain distributed problems are solvable while others are provably impossible, and how real-world systems navigate these theoretical constraints.","learning_objectives":["Students will master formal models of distributed computation and analyze consensus algorithms using rigorous mathematical frameworks","Students will apply theoretical impossibility results to evaluate the fundamental limits and trade-offs in distributed system design","Students will develop expertise in Byzantine fault tolerance mechanisms and their applications in modern distributed systems"],"prerequisites":"Data Structures and Algorithms, Discrete Mathematics, Operating Systems, and either Formal Methods or Theory of Computation","target_audience":"Upper-level undergraduate Computer Science students specializing in systems, distributed computing, or theoretical computer science"}

input_json: {"title":"Ethical AI Systems: From Bias Detection to Fair Algorithm Design","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This capstone course challenges students to confront the critical intersection of artificial intelligence and social responsibility. Students will develop, evaluate, and deploy AI systems while addressing real-world ethical challenges including algorithmic bias, fairness metrics, and responsible data governance. input_json: {"title":"Network Protocol Engineering and Performance Analysis Laboratory","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This intensive laboratory-driven course challenges students to design, implement, and optimize network protocols from the ground up. Students work in teams to build complete networking stacks, starting with raw socket programming and progressing to custom transport protocols, routing algorithms, and distributed system architectures. The course emphasizes hands-on protocol development using C/C++ and Python, with extensive performance benchmarking across simulated and real network environments. Weekly coding sprints require students to implement protocol features like congestion control, error correction, and security mechanisms while analyzing performance under various network conditions including high latency, packet loss, and bandwidth constraints. Students deploy their protocols on campus testbeds and cloud infrastructure, conducting rigorous performance comparisons against industry standards like TCP, UDP, and HTTP/3. The intensive nature includes 24-hour protocol hackathons, peer code reviews, and presentations to industry professionals. Final projects involve designing novel protocols for emerging applications such as IoT mesh networks, edge computing, or real-time gaming systems, with emphasis on scalability, reliability, and efficiency trade-offs.","learning_objectives":["Students will design and implement custom network protocols with advanced features like congestion control, flow control, and error recovery mechanisms","Students will conduct comprehensive performance analysis of networking systems using profiling tools, network simulators, and real-world testbed environments","Students will optimize network protocol performance through algorithmic improvements, system-level tuning, and architectural design decisions"],"prerequisites":"Computer Networks, Operating Systems, Data Structures and Algorithms, and proficiency in C/C++ programming with prior experience in socket programming","target_audience":"Advanced undergraduate Computer Science majors specializing in systems programming, network engineering, or distributed systems with strong programming backgrounds"}

input_json: {"title":"Building Resilient Distributed Systems: From Theory to Production","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This hands-on course explores the design, implementation, and deployment of fault-tolerant distributed systems that can withstand real-world failures. Students will build multiple distributed applications from scratch, learning to handle network partitions, server crashes, and scaling challenges through practical projects. The course emphasizes production-ready solutions, covering consistency models, replication strategies, load balancing, and monitoring systems. Students will work with modern tools like Docker, Kubernetes, message queues, and distributed databases while implementing consensus algorithms, distributed caching systems, and microservices architectures. Through weekly coding assignments and a capstone project deploying a multi-service application to cloud infrastructure, students gain deep understanding of trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. The curriculum bridges theoretical concepts like CAP theorem and Byzantine fault tolerance with practical implementation challenges, preparing students for systems engineering roles in industry. Projects include building a distributed key-value store, implementing Raft consensus algorithm, designing a fault-tolerant chat system, and creating auto-scaling web services that handle traffic spikes gracefully.","learning_objectives":["Students will design and implement distributed systems that gracefully handle various failure modes including network partitions, node crashes, and Byzantine faults","Students will apply consensus algorithms, replication strategies, and load balancing techniques to build production-ready scalable applications","Students will develop expertise in containerization, orchestration, and cloud deployment while mastering distributed systems monitoring and debugging methodologies"],"prerequisites":"Data Structures and Algorithms, Operating Systems, Computer Networks, and proficiency in at least one systems programming language (C++, Go, Rust, or Java)","target_audience":"Junior and senior Computer Science students interested in systems programming, cloud computing, or backend engineering careers"}

input_json: {"title":"Algorithmic Intelligence Across Domains: A Computational Survey","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This survey course explores how artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms are revolutionizing diverse computational domains beyond traditional CS applications. input_json: {"title":"Network Protocol Engineering: Building and Debugging Communication Systems","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This hands-on course immerses students in the practical design, implementation, and troubleshooting of network protocols and communication systems. Students will engineer custom protocols from scratch, analyze real-world network traffic, and solve complex connectivity challenges using industry-standard tools like Wireshark, GNS3, and Python socket programming. The curriculum emphasizes reverse-engineering existing protocols, implementing reliable data transfer mechanisms, and optimizing network performance under various conditions. input_json: {"title":"Formal Verification and Correctness in Large-Scale Software Systems","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course explores the mathematical foundations and theoretical frameworks for proving software correctness in complex, distributed systems. Students will study formal specification languages, model checking techniques, and theorem proving methodologies used to verify critical software properties. The curriculum emphasizes the theoretical underpinnings of program verification, including Hoare logic, temporal logic, and invariant analysis. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, students will examine how formal methods can guarantee system reliability, security, and performance in enterprise-level applications. Topics include abstract interpretation, bounded model checking, symbolic execution, and compositional verification techniques. The course addresses the theoretical challenges of scaling verification approaches to real-world software architectures, including microservices, concurrent systems, and safety-critical applications. Students will analyze case studies from aerospace, financial systems, and medical device software where formal verification is mandated. By the end of the course, students will understand the mathematical theory behind automated verification tools and the fundamental limitations of decidability in software verification problems.","learning_objectives":["Students will master formal specification languages and mathematical models for expressing software correctness properties","Students will apply theoretical verification techniques including model checking, theorem proving, and abstract interpretation to analyze software systems","Students will develop expertise in compositional verification methodologies for reasoning about large-scale distributed software architectures"],"prerequisites":"Discrete Mathematics, Data Structures and Algorithms, Programming Languages Theory, and Mathematical Logic","target_audience":"Upper-level undergraduate Computer Science majors planning careers in safety-critical software development, formal methods research, or graduate studies in software engineering"}

input_json: {"title":"Digital Infrastructure: From Silicon to Cloud Orchestration","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This comprehensive systems course bridges the gap between low-level hardware mechanisms and high-level distributed computing paradigms. input_json: {"title":"Digital Forensics and Cybercrime Investigation Fundamentals","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course introduces students to the fascinating world of digital forensics and cybercrime investigation through hands-on exploration of real-world security incidents. input_json: {"title":"Computational Intelligence: From Biological Inspiration to Algorithmic Innovation","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This foundational course explores how nature-inspired computational methods form the backbone of modern artificial intelligence systems. input_json: {"title":"Probabilistic Reasoning and Uncertainty Quantification in Intelligent Systems","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course explores the mathematical foundations of how intelligent systems handle uncertainty and make decisions under incomplete information. Students will delve into the theoretical underpinnings of probabilistic models, Bayesian inference, and uncertainty quantification techniques that power modern AI systems. The curriculum covers advanced topics including probabilistic graphical models, variational inference, Monte Carlo methods, and information-theoretic approaches to learning. Emphasis is placed on understanding the mathematical rigor behind uncertainty representation in machine learning algorithms, from naive Bayes classifiers to sophisticated neural network architectures with uncertainty estimation. Students will analyze the theoretical trade-offs between computational efficiency and accuracy in probabilistic reasoning, explore the convergence properties of sampling algorithms, and investigate the philosophical implications of uncertainty in artificial intelligence. The course bridges probability theory, statistics, and computer science to provide a comprehensive understanding of how machines can reason about uncertain worlds. Through rigorous mathematical analysis and proof-based assignments, students develop expertise in designing and analyzing probabilistic algorithms that form the backbone of modern AI systems, including autonomous vehicles, medical diagnosis systems, and financial modeling applications.","learning_objectives":["Students will master the mathematical foundations of probabilistic inference and develop proficiency in deriving and analyzing Bayesian learning algorithms","Students will apply advanced theoretical frameworks including variational methods and MCMC techniques to solve complex uncertainty quantification problems","Students will develop expertise in designing probabilistic models for real-world AI applications while understanding their theoretical limitations and convergence properties"],"prerequisites":"Calculus III (Multivariable Calculus), Linear Algebra, Probability and Statistics, Data Structures and Algorithms, and either Machine Learning Fundamentals or Artificial Intelligence","target_audience":"Upper-level undergraduate Computer Science majors with strong mathematical backgrounds, particularly those interested in AI research, graduate studies, or careers in machine learning engineering"}

The course emphasizes pattern recognition, strategic problem decomposition, and efficient implementation techniques across diverse algorithmic domains including dynamic programming, graph traversal, string manipulation, and advanced data structures. Students will build a portfolio of optimized solutions and develop the analytical thinking required to approach novel problems systematically. Students will delve into the convergence properties of gradient descent, universal approximation theorems, and the computational complexity of learning problems. Students will study the theoretical guarantees and limitations of deep learning architectures, including expressivity bounds, generalization theory, and the role of overparameterization in modern neural networks. The course bridges abstract mathematical concepts with practical AI systems by analyzing optimization landscapes, exploring the bias-variance tradeoff through a theoretical lens, and investigating the sample complexity requirements for various learning paradigms. input_json: {"title":"Competitive Programming and Algorithm Racing Laboratory","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This intensive laboratory course immerses students in the high-stakes world of competitive programming through hands-on algorithm implementation and optimization challenges. The lab environment emphasizes rapid prototyping, algorithmic pattern recognition, and performance optimization across diverse problem domains including graph theory, dynamic programming, computational geometry, and number theory. Each lab session presents progressively challenging problem sets that require students to analyze time and space complexity, implement efficient data structures, and debug solutions under pressure. Students participate in weekly mini-competitions, maintain detailed algorithm portfolios, and analyze winning solutions from international programming contests. input_json: {"title":"Distributed Systems Forensics and Performance Analysis","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This advanced course explores the intersection of distributed systems architecture and forensic analysis techniques. Students will learn to diagnose, analyze, and optimize complex distributed systems by examining system traces, network communications, and performance bottlenecks across multiple nodes. The course emphasizes hands-on investigation of real-world distributed system failures, teaching students to reconstruct system states from incomplete data, identify root causes of cascading failures, and develop monitoring strategies for large-scale deployments. Topics include distributed tracing methodologies, consensus protocol analysis, network partition recovery, Byzantine fault detection, and performance profiling in microservices architectures. Students will work with industry-standard tools like Jaeger, Prometheus, and custom instrumentation frameworks while developing their own forensic analysis tools. The course culminates in a capstone project where teams investigate a complex distributed system failure scenario, present their findings, and propose systematic improvements. This unique blend of systems engineering and investigative methodology prepares students for roles in site reliability engineering, distributed systems architecture, and high-performance computing environments.","learning_objectives":["Students will master distributed tracing and system observability techniques to reconstruct complex multi-node system behaviors","Students will apply forensic analysis methodologies to identify root causes of distributed system failures and performance degradation","Students will develop practical expertise in building monitoring infrastructure and automated failure detection systems for large-scale distributed environments"],"prerequisites":"Operating Systems, Computer Networks, Database Systems, and at least one course in distributed systems or concurrent programming","target_audience":"Senior computer science undergraduates interested in distributed systems, site reliability engineering, or systems architecture roles"}

input_json: {"title":"Real-Time Analytics Pipeline Engineering Lab","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This hands-on laboratory course immerses students in the design, implementation, and optimization of high-performance data pipelines for real-time analytics applications. Students work with streaming data architectures, distributed databases, and modern ETL/ELT frameworks to build scalable systems that process millions of records per second. The course emphasizes practical experience with technologies like Apache Kafka, Apache Spark, ClickHouse, and Redis, while exploring advanced topics including data partitioning strategies, query optimization for analytical workloads, and multi-database synchronization. Through weekly lab sessions, students construct end-to-end analytics platforms that ingest live data streams from APIs, social media feeds, and IoT sensors, then transform and store this data for immediate querying and visualization. Projects include building recommendation engines, fraud detection systems, and business intelligence dashboards that operate on continuously updating datasets. Students gain expertise in managing database clusters, implementing data quality monitoring, and designing fault-tolerant architectures. The laboratory environment simulates production conditions with high-volume data loads, teaching students to balance performance, consistency, and availability in distributed database systems while meeting strict latency requirements for real-time decision making.","learning_objectives":["Students will design and implement distributed database architectures capable of handling high-velocity data streams with sub-second latency requirements","Students will master real-time data pipeline technologies including stream processing frameworks, message queues, and analytical databases through intensive laboratory practice","Students will develop expertise in optimizing query performance across multiple database systems while maintaining data consistency in distributed environments"],"prerequisites":"Database Systems, Data Structures and Algorithms, Computer Networks, and proficiency in Python or Java programming","target_audience":"Junior and senior Computer Science students with interests in data engineering, distributed systems, or backend development who want hands-on experience with production-scale database technologies"}

input_json: {"title":"Real-Time Systems Programming for Interactive Media","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course explores the critical intersection of low-latency programming and multimedia applications, focusing on building responsive systems for gaming, audio processing, and live streaming platforms. Students will master techniques for managing memory allocation, thread synchronization, and hardware-level optimizations while developing interactive applications that demand consistent performance under strict timing constraints. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on programming with C++ and Rust, covering real-time scheduling algorithms, lock-free data structures, and SIMD optimization techniques. Projects include building a real-time audio synthesizer, developing a multiplayer game engine with sub-millisecond network latency, and creating a live video processing pipeline for content creators. Students will learn to profile system performance, identify bottlenecks, and implement solutions that maintain frame rates above 60 FPS while handling unpredictable user input and network conditions. input_json: {"title":"Database Ecosystems: From Relational Foundations to Modern Data Architectures","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This comprehensive survey course explores the evolution and diversity of database systems across traditional and contemporary computing environments. Students examine the historical progression from hierarchical and network models to relational databases, then venture into modern NoSQL paradigms, distributed systems, and cloud-native data solutions. The course covers key database families including document stores (MongoDB), key-value systems (Redis), column-family databases (Cassandra), graph databases (Neo4j), and time-series databases (InfluxDB). Students analyze real-world case studies demonstrating how organizations like Netflix, Amazon, and Google architect their data infrastructure. Topics include ACID vs. BASE consistency models, CAP theorem implications, database scaling strategies, data warehousing concepts, and emerging trends in serverless databases and edge computing. Through hands-on labs, students gain practical experience with multiple database technologies while developing the analytical skills to evaluate and recommend appropriate data storage solutions for diverse application requirements. The survey approach ensures broad exposure to database concepts without deep specialization, preparing students to make informed architectural decisions in their future careers.","learning_objectives":["Students will evaluate and compare different database paradigms including relational, document, key-value, column-family, and graph databases for specific use cases","Students will analyze the trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance in distributed database systems using CAP theorem principles","Students will design appropriate database architectures for various application scenarios by applying knowledge of scaling patterns, data modeling techniques, and performance considerations"],"prerequisites":"Data Structures and Algorithms, Object-Oriented Programming, and basic understanding of computer networks and operating systems concepts","target_audience":"Junior and senior Computer Science majors who have completed core programming courses and seek broad exposure to database technologies before specializing in software engineering, data science, or systems architecture"}

input_json: {"title":"Formal Methods for Reliable Software Systems","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course explores the mathematical foundations and theoretical frameworks used to specify, design, and verify software systems with high reliability requirements. Students will study formal specification languages, model checking techniques, and theorem proving methods to analyze software correctness. The curriculum covers temporal logic, process algebras, and state-based specification methods including Z notation and Alloy. Emphasis is placed on understanding how formal verification can prevent critical software failures in safety-critical systems such as medical devices, aerospace applications, and financial trading platforms. Students will learn to model concurrent systems, verify properties like deadlock freedom and mutual exclusion, and understand the trade-offs between automated verification tools and manual proof techniques. The course examines real-world case studies where formal methods have successfully identified critical bugs that traditional testing missed, as well as the practical challenges of integrating formal verification into industrial software development processes. By the end of the course, students will possess a deep theoretical understanding of how mathematical rigor can be applied to ensure software reliability and will be prepared for advanced study in software verification or careers in high-assurance software development.","learning_objectives":["Students will master formal specification techniques using mathematical notation to precisely describe software behavior and system requirements","Students will apply model checking and theorem proving methodologies to verify critical properties of concurrent and distributed software systems","Students will develop expertise in analyzing the theoretical foundations of software correctness and understanding the computational complexity of verification problems"],"prerequisites":"Discrete Mathematics, Data Structures and Algorithms, Programming Languages Theory, and Mathematical Logic or Automata Theory","target_audience":"Junior and senior Computer Science majors interested in software reliability, system verification, or pursuing graduate studies in formal methods"}

input_json: {"title":"Real-Time Data Stream Processing and Event-Driven Database Architectures","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This specialized course explores the cutting-edge intersection of streaming data technologies and modern database systems. Students dive deep into real-time data processing frameworks like Apache Kafka, Apache Storm, and Apache Flink, while mastering event-driven database architectures that power today's high-velocity applications. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on experience with time-series databases, streaming analytics, and complex event processing (CEP) systems. Students will design and implement scalable data pipelines that handle millions of events per second, working with technologies like InfluxDB, Apache Cassandra, and Redis Streams. The course covers critical concepts including data partitioning strategies, eventual consistency models, and fault-tolerant distributed systems. Real-world case studies from finance (high-frequency trading), IoT (sensor networks), social media (live feeds), and gaming (real-time leaderboards) provide practical context. By course completion, students will possess the specialized skills to architect and maintain the data infrastructure that powers modern real-time applications, understanding both the theoretical foundations and practical implementation challenges of streaming data systems.","learning_objectives":["Students will master real-time data stream processing frameworks and implement fault-tolerant event-driven database systems","Students will apply specialized streaming analytics techniques to solve complex temporal data challenges in distributed environments","Students will develop practical expertise in designing scalable data pipelines for high-velocity applications using modern streaming technologies"],"prerequisites":"Database Systems, Data Structures and Algorithms, Operating Systems, and familiarity with distributed computing concepts","target_audience":"Upper-level computer science undergraduates interested in big data, distributed systems, or backend engineering roles in tech companies"}

input_json: {"title":"Distributed Database Systems: Scalability, Consistency, and Performance Optimization","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This advanced course explores the complex challenges of designing, implementing, and managing distributed database systems in modern computing environments. Students will delve deep into the theoretical foundations and practical implementations of distributed data storage, focusing on critical trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance (CAP theorem). The curriculum covers advanced topics including distributed transaction processing, consensus algorithms, data partitioning strategies, replication mechanisms, and fault tolerance. Students will work extensively with NoSQL databases, distributed SQL systems, and emerging technologies like blockchain-based databases. Through hands-on projects, students will build their own distributed database components, analyze performance bottlenecks, and implement optimization strategies for real-world scenarios. input_json: {"title":"Algorithmic Problem Solving Across Domains: From Games to Genomics","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This survey course explores how algorithmic thinking and design principles apply across diverse problem domains, from recreational puzzles to cutting-edge scientific applications. input_json: {"title":"Digital Infrastructure Foundations: Building the Modern Computing Ecosystem","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This course demystifies the invisible infrastructure that powers our digital world by examining how computers communicate, store data, and work together as systems. Students explore the fundamental building blocks of computing ecosystems, from understanding how data travels across networks to how operating systems manage computer resources. Through hands-on labs and practical projects, students build their own simple network services, configure virtual machines, and trace the journey of data from application to hardware. The course emphasizes real-world problem-solving by examining case studies of system failures, performance bottlenecks, and scalability challenges faced by companies like Netflix, Google, and banking institutions. Students learn to think like systems architects, considering trade-offs between performance, reliability, and cost. Topics include computer architecture basics, network protocols, file systems, virtualization, cloud computing concepts, and system security fundamentals. By course completion, students understand how individual computers become powerful distributed systems and gain practical skills in Linux command line, basic networking tools, and system monitoring. This foundation prepares students for advanced courses in operating systems, distributed systems, and network security while providing valuable practical skills for internships and entry-level positions.","learning_objectives":["Students will analyze and explain how computer systems interact within larger computing infrastructures and networks","Students will design and implement basic network services and system configurations using industry-standard tools and practices","Students will evaluate system performance and reliability trade-offs to make informed architectural decisions in computing environments"],"prerequisites":"Completion of CS fundamentals (data structures and algorithms), basic proficiency in at least one programming language (preferably Python or Java), and introductory discrete mathematics","target_audience":"Second-year Computer Science majors and related engineering students who have completed introductory programming courses"}

input_json: {"title":"Digital Communication Protocols and Network Architecture","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This foundational course explores how computers communicate across networks, from local area networks to the global Internet. Students will examine the layered architecture of network protocols, starting with physical transmission of digital signals and progressing through data link, network, transport, and application layers. The course emphasizes hands-on exploration of protocol behavior through packet analysis, network simulation, and programming exercises. Key topics include Ethernet switching, IP routing, TCP reliability mechanisms, DNS resolution, and HTTP web protocols. Students will build simple network applications using socket programming and analyze real network traffic using tools like Wireshark. The course balances theoretical understanding of protocol design principles with practical skills in network troubleshooting and performance analysis. input_json: {"title":"Approximation Algorithms for NP-Hard Optimization Problems","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This advanced course explores sophisticated algorithmic techniques for tackling computationally intractable optimization problems that arise in real-world applications. Students will study the theory and practice of approximation algorithms, learning to design efficient solutions that provide provable performance guarantees for problems where optimal solutions are computationally infeasible. The curriculum covers fundamental approximation techniques including greedy algorithms, linear programming relaxations, semidefinite programming, randomized rounding, and primal-dual methods. Students will analyze classic problems such as facility location, network design, scheduling, and graph partitioning, developing algorithms with proven approximation ratios. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations\u2014including hardness of approximation results and the PCP theorem\u2014and practical implementation challenges. Advanced topics include online algorithms, mechanism design, and recent developments in streaming algorithms for massive datasets. Students will complete a substantial research project implementing and evaluating approximation algorithms on real problem instances, bridging the gap between theoretical computer science and practical algorithm engineering. This course prepares students for graduate research in algorithms or careers in optimization-heavy industries.","learning_objectives":["Students will master advanced approximation algorithm design techniques including LP relaxations, randomized rounding, and primal-dual methods for solving NP-hard optimization problems","Students will apply rigorous mathematical analysis to prove approximation ratios and understand fundamental limits of polynomial-time approximability","Students will develop practical expertise in implementing and evaluating approximation algorithms on real-world problem instances and large-scale datasets"],"prerequisites":"Advanced Data Structures and Algorithms, Discrete Mathematics, Linear Algebra, Mathematical Probability, and Computational Complexity Theory","target_audience":"Senior computer science undergraduates with strong mathematical backgrounds, particularly those interested in theoretical computer science, operations research, or algorithm-intensive software engineering roles"}

input_json: {"title":"Adversarial Machine Learning and AI Security Exploitation","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This advanced course explores the vulnerability landscape of artificial intelligence systems and machine learning models through an adversarial lens. Students will learn to identify, exploit, and defend against sophisticated attacks targeting AI systems, including adversarial examples, model inversion attacks, data poisoning, and neural network backdoors. The course combines theoretical foundations with hands-on experience in crafting adversarial inputs, implementing evasion techniques against real-world ML systems, and developing robust defensive mechanisms. Students will work with cutting-edge research in AI security, analyzing case studies from autonomous vehicles, facial recognition systems, and natural language processing applications. The curriculum covers advanced topics such as gradient-based attack methods, generative adversarial networks for security applications, federated learning vulnerabilities, and privacy-preserving machine learning techniques. Through practical labs, students will use frameworks like CleverHans, Foolbox, and Adversarial Robustness Toolbox to conduct security assessments of popular ML models. input_json: {"title":"Bayesian Modeling and Uncertainty Quantification in Modern Data Systems","domain":"computer_science","level":"undergraduate","duration":"semester","description":"This advanced course explores the critical role of uncertainty quantification in data science through the lens of Bayesian statistical methodology. Students will delve into hierarchical modeling, Monte Carlo methods, and probabilistic programming to address real-world problems where uncertainty is inherent and must be rigorously quantified. The course emphasizes the transition from frequentist to Bayesian thinking, covering advanced topics including variational inference, Gaussian processes, and Bayesian neural networks. Through hands-on projects with complex, messy datasets from domains like climate science, finance, and healthcare, students will learn to build models that not only make predictions but also communicate the confidence and uncertainty in those predictions. Special attention is given to computational challenges, including MCMC diagnostics, model comparison using information criteria, and scalable approximate inference methods. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to tackle high-stakes data science problems where understanding and communicating uncertainty is as important as point estimates, preparing them for roles in research, risk assessment, and decision-making under uncertainty.","learning_objectives":["Students will master Bayesian inference techniques including MCMC sampling, variational inference, and probabilistic programming using tools like Stan and PyMC","Students will apply hierarchical modeling and Gaussian processes to complex, multi-level data structures with appropriate uncertainty quantification","Students will develop expertise in model criticism, comparison, and validation within the Bayesian framework for high-stakes decision making"],"prerequisites":"Multivariate Calculus, Linear Algebra, Probability Theory, Statistical Inference, and proficiency in Python or R programming","target_audience":"Advanced undergraduate students in statistics, mathematics, computer science, or engineering with strong mathematical background seeking specialization in probabilistic modeling"}
